_readme: Sample question bank. surface = everything the player and the agent can see in the wallet popup; simulation = the balance / authority changes returned by the paid simulation check (not sent before answering); truth and lesson are returned only after answering. case references taxonomy.json. defaults are merged into every question's surface. Instruction field conventions are in docs/edge-cases.md.

questions.title: Claim JUP airdrop
questions.lesson: Claiming an airdrop never requires you to approve anything. Approve hands someone else “the right to spend your money”; the transaction itself moves nothing, so the wallet simulation looks perfectly calm.

questions.title: Jupiter swap 1 SOL
questions.lesson: Many instructions does not mean danger. Check each recipient: the SOL goes into your own wSOL account, the close refunds to you, and the router is the verified Jupiter program.

questions.title: Send 500 USDC to Alice
questions.lesson: Address poisoning: the first 4 and last 4 characters match Alice, the middle does not. Before copying an address from history, compare the full string against your address book.

questions.title: Claim free Mad Lads pass

surface.prompt: Claim your free Mad Lads pass

questions.lesson: Money can be taken without changing the owner: when the wSOL account is closed, its 8.2 SOL in lamports goes to whoever closes it. Handing any SetAuthority authorityType to someone else means losing control.

questions.title: Sign to verify wallet

surface.prompt: Your wallet will be suspended in 10 minutes. Sign to verify wallet ownership.

simulation.notes: Wallet simulation failed because a durable nonce transaction needs the blockhash stored in the nonce account; re-simulating with replaceRecentBlockhash shows 12.4 SOL leaving

questions.lesson: “Verifying a wallet” never needs a transaction; signing a message is enough. A durable nonce transaction is not broadcast right away; the other party sends it days later, after you have forgotten what you signed.

questions.title: Gasless claim

surface.prompt: Gasless claim — 0 fee, sponsored by us

questions.lesson: Who pays the gas does not matter; who signs does. The other party being fee payer only means they are willing to spend 0.000005 SOL to take your 1500 USDC.

questions.title: Claim staking rewards

simulation.notes: Lookup table entry 3 resolves to DrA1nMkQ…

questions.lesson: When the wallet shows “unknown account”, that account is the most important thing in the whole transaction. An amount exactly equal to all your USDC is no coincidence either.

questions.title: Register alice.sol domain
questions.lesson: You can be drained with no transfer instruction at all: priority fee = units × microLamports. Whenever you see SetComputeUnitPrice, do the math.

questions.title: Jupiter swap 0.5 SOL (official domain)
questions.lesson: Right domain ≠ right transaction. When the frontend is poisoned (DNS hijack, malicious dependency, browser extension) the domain check is all green; the last line of defense is always the instructions themselves: a Jupiter SOL→USDC swap never needs you to approve USDC.

questions.title: Buy MOON token
questions.lesson: The transaction itself is completely normal; the trap is the asset you buy. MOON's freeze authority and permanentDelegate are both a hot wallet, so the issuer can freeze your account or pull the tokens at any time. Check the mint before buying, not just the transaction.

questions.title: Free mint pass
questions.lesson: This is how a real drainer takes everything at once: approve, transfer, change ownership, and close account crammed into one transaction. Something “free” should not need four instructions.

questions.title: Mint DegenApe

simulation.notes: Only SOL flows out; no asset flows in

questions.lesson: A mint always has a mint instruction (a call to a program like Candy Machine or Token Metadata). A single transfer to a plain address is paying without receiving.

questions.title: Migrate stake to a high-yield validator

surface.prompt: Migrate your stake to a 9.2% APY validator

questions.lesson: Switching validators uses Delegate / Deactivate; it never changes the Withdrawer. Whoever holds the Withdrawer authority owns the staked SOL.

questions.title: Jupiter swap (subdomain)

simulation.notes: SOL flows out; no USDC flows in

questions.lesson: Two lookalikes stacked: the domain starts with jup.ag but the root domain is swap-app.com; the program ID shares its first 7 characters with Jupiter but differs after that. Compare program IDs in full.

questions.title: Orca swap 100 USDC
questions.lesson: The Orca program is real; the smuggled “network fee” is fake. Network fees never go through a Transfer instruction, and 4.9 SOL is 98% of your balance.

questions.title: Raydium swap 100 USDC → RAY
questions.lesson: An Approve is not automatically dangerous: the amount equals the trade exactly, the delegate is Raydium's program authority, and the transaction ends with a Revoke. This is the standard pattern for older AMMs.

questions.title: Clean up 3 spam NFTs

surface.prompt: Burn 3 spam NFTs and reclaim 0.006 SOL rent

questions.lesson: Burn and CloseAccount both sound scary, but what burns is spam and the rent refunds to you. Judging a CloseAccount comes down to one thing: is the destination you.

questions.title: Sign in to Drift

simulation.notes: Plaintext message, not a transaction; no balance changes

questions.lesson: SIWS plaintext sign-in is harmless: the message is not a transaction and cannot land on-chain even when signed. The only thing to check is that the domain in the message matches the page's domain.

questions.title: Deposit 200 USDC to Binance
questions.lesson: The extra CreateAssociatedTokenAccount and 0.002 SOL are rent for creating the recipient's USDC account; the recipient's full address matches your address book.

questions.title: Revoke all approvals in one click
questions.lesson: The button says Revoke; the instruction type is ApproveChecked. A real revoke is a Revoke instruction, with no delegate and no amount.

questions.title: Revoke USDC approval
questions.lesson: The only difference from the previous kind of question is the instruction type: Revoke has just two accounts, source and owner, so it cannot give money to anyone.

questions.title: Sign message to verify

surface.prompt: Sign this message to verify you own the wallet

simulation.notes: Simulating the “message” bytes as a transaction: 12.4 SOL leaves

questions.lesson: Signing a message is harmless, provided it really is a message. If the bytes deserialize into a transaction, your signature is a transaction signature. Legitimate sign-in uses SIWS plaintext.

questions.title: Jupiter swap 10 SOL (slippage)

simulation.notes: There are no sandwich bots in simulation, so it looks like you get 1470 USDC; on-chain, minOut = 0 means receiving 0 still counts as success

questions.lesson: Right program, right domain, simulation looks right too; only minOut = 0 is wrong. This is a tampered frontend or browser extension; the slippage parameter is your only protection.

questions.title: Mint Okay Bear
questions.lesson: The page says 0.1 SOL; the instruction says 1.0 SOL. Compare the number in the copy with the number in the transaction; it is off by one decimal point.

questions.title: Marinade stake 5 SOL
questions.lesson: The program check shows Marinade is upgradeable. Upgradeable is not a red flag; a hot wallet as upgrade authority is. Here it is a multisig.

questions.title: Send Alice 0.5 SOL rent
questions.lesson: Memo and Compute Budget are the two most common “unfamiliar programs”, and neither touches assets. The recipient's full address matches your address book.

questions.title: Jupiter swap 2 SOL (simulation failed)

simulation.notes: The wallet's simulation failed on an expired blockhash; re-simulation is normal

questions.lesson: A failed wallet simulation means “cannot see”, not “something is wrong”. When every instruction checks out, one re-simulation is enough; do not reject a normal transaction over a single red warning.

questions.title: List Mad Lads for sale
questions.lesson: An amount of just 1 looks restrained, but the delegate is a plain wallet, not the marketplace program's PDA. Legitimate marketplaces delegate the NFT to a program authority; a wallet address holding the delegation can transfer it away directly.

questions.title: Burn spam NFT to claim 50 USDC

surface.prompt: Burn your spam NFT to claim 50 USDC reward

questions.lesson: The first Burn is real and harmless; its job is to make you think “this is just cleanup”. The second instruction hands ownership of your USDC account to someone else. Read through the last instruction before signing.

questions.title: Jupiter swap 1 SOL (homoglyph domain)
questions.lesson: The second letter of the domain is the Greek letter υ, invisible to the eye. Checking a domain for non-ASCII characters is free for a program; a human can only rely on bookmarks.

questions.title: Deposit into yield vault

surface.prompt: Deposit 1,000 USDC into Vault v2 (12% APY)

simulation.notes: Inner CPI: SPL Token TransferChecked 1000 USDC → AtKrUsdcAta… (the authority collector's account); no receipt token flows in

questions.lesson: The instruction list is spotless: just one “program call”. The transfer happens inside the program via CPI, invisible in the popup; simulation shows 1000 USDC gone and nothing coming in. A vault deposit always has share tokens flowing in.

questions.title: Jupiter swap 1 SOL → “USDC”
questions.lesson: The Jupiter program is real, and it will route any token. The “USDC” you receive is a different mint; a symbol can be anything. Official USDC has exactly one mint (EPjF…Dt1v).

questions.title: Marinade delayed unstake 4.2 mSOL

simulation.notes: Created a ticket account (owner is the Marinade program); 4.98 SOL can be claimed after 2 epochs

questions.lesson: Delayed unstake burns the mSOL first and gives you a ticket; the SOL arrives two epochs later. “Out but nothing in” is normal in simulation: the ticket account is the receipt, and its owner is the Marinade program, not some wallet.
